title: The Introduction
paragraphs: Nature (the art by which God has made and governs the world) is imitated by the art of man in many things, and in this one too: that human art can make an Artificial Animal. For since life is but a motion of limbs, beginning in some principal part within, why may we not say that all Automata (engines that move themselves by springs and wheels, as a watch does) have an artificial life? For what is the heart but a spring; the nerves but so many strings; the joints but so many wheels, giving motion to the whole body just as the maker intended? Art goes further still, imitating that rational and most excellent work of Nature, Man. For by art is created that great LEVIATHAN called a COMMON-WEALTH, or STATE (in Latin CIVITAS), which is but an Artificial Man, though of greater stature and strength than the natural one, for whose protection and defence it was intended. In it, the Sovereignty is an Artificial Soul, giving life and motion to the whole body; the magistrates and other officers of judicature and execution are artificial joints; reward and punishment (by which, fastened to the seat of the Sovereignty, every joint and member is moved to perform its duty) are the nerves that do the same in the natural body; the wealth and riches of all the particular members are the strength; Salus Populi (the people's safety) is its business; counsellors, by whom all things needful for it to know are suggested to it, are the memory; equity and laws are an artificial reason and will; concord is its health; sedition its sickness; and civil war its death. Lastly, the pacts and covenants by which the parts of this Body Politic were at first made, set together, and united resemble that Fiat, or the Let Us Make Man, pronounced by God in the Creation.
First, the matter of it, and the maker, both of which is Man.
Secondly, how and by what covenants it is made; what the rights and just power or authority of a Sovereign are; and what preserves it and dissolves it.

Concerning the first, there is a saying much abused of late, that wisdom is acquired not by reading books but by reading men. As a consequence, those persons who for the most part can give no other proof of being wise take great delight in showing what they think they have read in men, by uncharitable censures of one another behind their backs. But there is another saying, not understood of late, by which they might learn truly to read one another, if they would take the pains; and that is, Nosce Teipsum, Read Thy Self. This was not meant, as it is now used, to countenance either the barbarous behaviour of men in power towards their inferiors, or to encourage men of low degree to a saucy behaviour towards their betters. Rather, it was meant to teach us that, because of the similarity between the thoughts and passions of one man and the thoughts and passions of another, whoever looks into himself and considers what he does when he thinks, opines, reasons, hopes, fears, etc., and on what grounds, will thereby read and know what the thoughts and passions of all other men are, on similar occasions. I mean the similarity of the passions, which are the same in all men—desire, fear, hope, etc.—not the similarity of the objects of the passions, which are the things desired, feared, hoped for, etc. For these the individual constitution and particular education make vary so widely, and they are so easily kept hidden from us, that the characters of a man's heart, blotted and confounded as they are by dissembling, lying, counterfeiting, and erroneous doctrines, are legible only to Him who searches hearts. And although by men's actions we sometimes discover their designs, yet to do this without comparing them with our own, and distinguishing all the circumstances by which the case may come to be altered, is to decipher without a key, and to be for the most part deceived, by too much trust or by too much diffidence, depending on whether the reader himself is a good or an evil man.

But let one man read another by his actions ever so perfectly, it serves him only with his acquaintances, who are but few. He that is to govern a whole nation must read in himself not this or that particular man, but Mankind. That is hard to do—harder than learning any language or science. Yet when I have set down my own reading orderly and clearly, the pains left to another will only be to consider whether he does not find the same in himself. For this kind of doctrine admits of no other demonstration.

title: Chapter 1. Of Sense
paragraphs: Concerning the thoughts of man, I will consider them first singly, and afterwards in a train, or as they depend upon one another. Taken singly, each one is a representation or appearance of some quality, or other accident, of a body outside us, which is commonly called an Object. This Object works on the eyes, ears, and other parts of a man's body; and by the diversity of its working, it produces a diversity of appearances.

The origin of them all is what we call Sense (for there is no conception in a man's mind that has not, at first, either totally or in parts, been begotten upon the organs of Sense). The rest are derived from that original.

To know the natural cause of Sense is not very necessary to the business now in hand, and I have written about it at length elsewhere. Nevertheless, to fill out each part of my present method, I will briefly state it in this place.

The cause of Sense is the external body, or Object, which presses on the organ proper to each sense, either immediately (as in taste and touch) or mediately (as in seeing, hearing, and smelling). This pressure, through the mediation of nerves and other strings and membranes of the body, is continued inwards to the brain and heart, where it causes a resistance, or counter-pressure, or endeavour of the heart to relieve itself. Because this endeavour is outward, it seems to be some matter outside us. And this seeming, or Fancy, is what men call Sense; consisting, for the eye, in a light or coloured figure; for the ear, in a sound; for the nostril, in an odour; for the tongue and palate, in a savour; and for the rest of the body, in heat, cold, hardness, softness, and other such qualities as we discern by feeling. All these qualities, called sensible, are in the object that causes them merely so many several motions of matter, by which it presses our organs in various ways. And in us who are pressed, they are nothing else but various motions (for motion produces nothing but motion). But their appearance to us is Fancy—the same waking as dreaming. And just as pressing, rubbing, or striking the eye makes us fancy a light, and pressing the ear produces a din, so the bodies we see or hear also produce the same effects by their strong though unobserved action. For if those colours and sounds were in the bodies or objects that cause them, they could not be separated from them, as we see by glasses, and in echoes by reflection, that they are: we know that the thing we see is in one place and its appearance in another. And though at some certain distance the real and very object seems clothed with the fancy it begets in us, still the object is one thing and the image or fancy is another. So that Sense, in all cases, is nothing else but original fancy, caused (as I have said) by the pressure—that is, by the motion—of external things upon our eyes, ears, and other organs ordained for that purpose.

But the philosophy-schools, throughout all the universities of Christendom, grounded on certain texts of Aristotle, teach a different doctrine. They say that the cause of vision is that the thing seen sends out on every side a Visible Species (in English, a Visible Show, Apparition, or Aspect, or a Being Seen); and that the receiving of this into the eye is seeing. As for the cause of hearing, they say the thing heard sends out an Audible Species—that is, an Audible Aspect, or Audible Being Seen—which, entering the ear, produces hearing. And as for the cause of understanding, they also say that the thing understood sends out Intelligible Species, that is, an Intelligible Being Seen, which, coming into the understanding, makes us understand. I do not say this as if I disapproved of the use of universities; but because I shall have to speak hereafter of their office in a Commonwealth, I must let you see on every occasion in passing what things in them stand in need of amendment—among which the frequency of meaningless speech is one.

title: Chapter 2. Of Imagination
paragraphs: That when a thing lies still, unless something else stirs it, it will lie still forever, is a truth no man doubts. But that when a thing is in motion, it will be in motion eternally, unless something else stops it—though the reason is the same (namely, that nothing can change itself)—is not so easily assented to. For men measure not only other men but all other things by themselves; and because they find themselves subject after motion to pain and weariness, they think every other thing also grows weary of motion and seeks rest of its own accord, hardly considering whether the desire for rest they find in themselves does not itself consist in some other motion. From this it is that the Schools say that heavy bodies fall downwards out of an appetite for rest, and to conserve their nature in the place most proper for them—absurdly ascribing appetite, and knowledge of what is good for their conservation (which is more than man has) to inanimate things.

When a body is once in motion, it moves (unless something else hinders it) eternally; and whatever hinders it cannot extinguish it in an instant, but only in time and by degrees. And as we see in water, that though the wind ceases, the waves do not stop rolling for a long time after, so it also happens with the motion that is made in the internal parts of a man when he sees, dreams, etc. For after the object is removed, or the eye shut, we still retain an image of the thing seen, though more obscure than when we see it. And this is what the Latins call Imagination, from the image made in seeing; and they apply the term, though improperly, to all the other senses. But the Greeks call it Fancy, which signifies appearance, and is as proper to one sense as to another. Imagination, therefore, is nothing but decaying sense, and is found in men and in many other living creatures, both sleeping and waking.

The decay of sense in waking men is not the decay of the motion made in sense, but an obscuring of it, in the manner that the light of the sun obscures the light of the stars; for the stars exercise the power by which they are visible no less by day than by night. But because, among the many strokes that our eyes, ears, and other organs receive from external bodies, only the predominant is sensible, the light of the sun being predominant, we are not affected by the action of the stars. And though an object that is removed from our eyes leaves an impression in us, yet other objects more present, succeeding and working upon us, obscure the imagination of the past, and make it weak, just as a man's voice is in the noise of the day. From this it follows that the longer the time after the sight or sense of any object, the weaker is the imagination. For the continual change of a man's body destroys in time the parts that were moved in sense; so that distance of time and distance of place have one and the same effect in us. For just as at a distance in place, what we look at appears dim and without distinction of smaller parts, and as voices grow weak and inarticulate, so also after great distance in time, our imagination of the past is weak; and we lose, for example, of cities we have seen, many particular streets; and of actions, many particular circumstances. This decaying sense, when we want to express the thing itself (I mean Fancy itself), we call Imagination, as I said before; but when we want to express the decay, and signify that the sense is fading, old, and past, it is called Memory. So that Imagination and Memory are but one thing, which for various considerations has various names.

Much memory, or memory of many things, is called Experience. Again, Imagination is only of those things that have formerly been perceived by sense, either all at once or in parts at several times. The first (imagining the whole object as it was presented to the sense) is Simple Imagination, as when one imagines a man or a horse one has seen before. The other is Compound, as when, from the sight of a man at one time, and of a horse at another, we conceive in our mind a centaur. So when a man compounds the image of his own person with the image of the actions of another man—as when a man imagines himself a Hercules, or an Alexander (which often happens to those much taken with the reading of Romances)—it is a compound imagination, and properly nothing but a fiction of the mind. There are also other imaginations that rise in men (though waking) from the great impression made in sense; as from gazing on the sun, the impression leaves an image of the sun before our eyes a long time after; and from being long and intently fixed on geometrical figures, a man in the dark (though awake) will have the images of lines and angles before his eyes—a kind of fancy that has no particular name, being something that does not commonly enter into men's discourse.

The imaginations of those who sleep are what we call Dreams. And these too (like all other imaginations) have been before, either totally or in parts, in the sense. And because in sleep the brain and nerves, which are the necessary organs of sense, are so numbed as not to be easily moved by the action of external objects, there can occur in sleep no imagination, and therefore no dream, except what proceeds from the agitation of the inward parts of a man's body—which inward parts, because of the connection they have with the brain and other organs, when they are disordered, keep these in motion; whereby the imaginations formerly made there appear as if a man were awake, except that, the organs of sense being now numbed so that there is no new object that can master and obscure them with a more vigorous impression, a dream must necessarily be more vivid, in this silence of sense, than our waking thoughts. And so it comes about that it is a difficult thing, and by many thought impossible, to distinguish exactly between sense and dreaming. For my part, when I consider that in dreams I do not often, nor consistently, think of the same persons, places, objects, and actions as I do waking, nor remember so long a train of coherent thoughts when dreaming as at other times; and because waking I often observe the absurdity of dreams, but never dream of the absurdities of my waking thoughts; I am well satisfied that, being awake, I know I do not dream, though when I dream, I think myself awake.

And since dreams are caused by the disorder of some of the inward parts of the body, various disorders must necessarily cause different dreams. Hence it is that lying cold breeds dreams of fear, and raises the thought and image of some fearful object (the motion from the brain to the inner parts, and from the inner parts to the brain, being reciprocal); and that, as anger causes heat in some parts of the body when we are awake, so when we sleep, the overheating of those same parts causes anger, and raises up in the brain the imagination of an enemy. In the same way, as natural kindness, when we are awake, causes desire, and desire makes heat in certain other parts of the body, so too much heat in those parts while we sleep raises in the brain an imagination of some kindness shown. In sum, our dreams are the reverse of our waking imaginations; the motion, when we are awake, beginning at one end, and when we dream, at the other.

The most difficult discerning of a man's dream from his waking thoughts is when, by some accident, we do not notice that we have slept—which is easy to happen to a man full of fearful thoughts, and whose conscience is much troubled, and who sleeps without the usual circumstances of going to bed or taking off his clothes, as one that nods in a chair. For he who takes pains, and lays himself down on purpose to sleep, in case some strange and extravagant fancy comes to him, cannot easily think it anything but a dream. We read of Marcus Brutus (one whose life was given him by Julius Caesar, and was also his favourite, and who nevertheless murdered him), how at Philippi, the night before he gave battle to Augustus Caesar, he saw a fearful apparition, which is commonly related by historians as a vision; but considering the circumstances, one may easily judge it to have been but a short dream. For sitting in his tent, pensive and troubled with the horror of his rash act, it was not hard for him, slumbering in the cold, to dream of what most frightened him; and this fear, as by degrees it made him wake, must also have made the apparition by degrees vanish. And having no assurance that he had slept, he could have no cause to think it a dream, or anything but a vision. And this is no very rare incident: for even those who are perfectly awake, if they are timorous and superstitious, possessed with fearful tales, and alone in the dark, are subject to the like fancies, and believe they see spirits and dead men's ghosts walking in churchyards; whereas it is either only their fancy, or else the knavery of such persons as make use of such superstitious fear to pass disguised in the night to places where they would not be known to go.

From this ignorance of how to distinguish dreams, and other strong fancies, from vision and sense, arose the greatest part of the religion of the Gentiles in times past, who worshipped Satyrs, Fauns, Nymphs, and the like; and nowadays the opinion that rude people have of Fairies, Ghosts, and Goblins, and of the power of Witches. For as for witches, I do not think that their witchcraft is any real power; but yet that they are justly punished for the false belief they have, that they can do such mischief, joined with their purpose to do it if they can—their trade being nearer to a new religion than to a craft or science. And as for fairies and walking ghosts, the opinion of them has, I think, been deliberately either taught, or not contradicted, to keep in credit the use of exorcism, of crosses, of holy water, and other such inventions of ghostly men. Nevertheless, there is no doubt that God can make supernatural apparitions. But that he does so often, so that men need to fear such things more than they fear the staying or changing of the course of Nature (which he can also stay and change), is no point of Christian faith. But evil men, under the pretext that God can do anything, are so bold as to say anything when it serves their turn, though they think it untrue: it is the part of a wise man to believe them no further than right reason makes what they say appear credible. If this superstitious fear of spirits were taken away, and with it the prognostications from dreams, false prophecies, and many other things depending on them, by which crafty ambitious persons abuse simple people, men would be much fitter than they are for civil obedience.

And this ought to be the work of the Schools; but they rather nourish such doctrine. For (not knowing what imagination or the senses are) what they receive they teach: some saying that imaginations rise of themselves and have no cause; others, that they rise most commonly from the will; and that good thoughts are blown (inspired) into a man by God, and evil thoughts by the Devil; or that good thoughts are poured (infused) into a man by God, and evil ones by the Devil. Some say the senses receive the Species of things, and deliver them to the Common-sense; and the Common-sense delivers them over to the Fancy, and the Fancy to the Memory, and the Memory to the Judgment—like handing of things from one to another, with many words making nothing understood.

The imagination that is raised in a man (or any other creature endowed with the faculty of imagining) by words, or other voluntary signs, is what we generally call Understanding; and it is common to man and beast. For a dog by custom will understand the call, or the scolding, of his master; and so will many other beasts. That understanding which is peculiar to man is the understanding not only of his will but of his conceptions and thoughts, by the sequence and connection of the names of things into affirmations, negations, and other forms of speech; and of this kind of understanding I shall speak hereafter.

title: Chapter 3. Of the Consequence or Train of Imaginations
paragraphs: By Consequence, or Train of Thoughts, I mean that succession of one thought to another which is called (to distinguish it from discourse in words) Mental Discourse.

When a man thinks of anything whatsoever, his next thought after is not altogether as accidental as it seems to be. Not every thought succeeds to every other thought indifferently. But just as we have no imagination of which we have not formerly had sense, in whole or in part, so we have no transition from one imagination to another of which we never had the like before in our senses. The reason for this is as follows. All fancies are motions within us, relics of those made in sense; and those motions that immediately succeeded one another in sense continue together also after sense; so that when the former comes again to take place and be predominant, the latter follows, by the coherence of the matter moved—in the same way water on a flat table is drawn whichever way any one part of it is guided by the finger. But because in sense, to one and the same thing perceived, sometimes one thing, sometimes another succeeds, it comes about in time that, in imagining anything, there is no certainty what we shall imagine next; only this is certain: it will be something that has succeeded the same thing before, at one time or another.

This train of thoughts, or mental discourse, is of two sorts. The first is Unguided, without design, and inconstant, in which there is no passionate thought to govern and direct those that follow it as the end and goal of some desire or other passion: in such a case, the thoughts are said to wander, and seem unconnected one to another, as in a dream. Such are commonly the thoughts of men who are not only without company but also without care for anything; though even then their thoughts are as busy as at other times, but without harmony, like the sound that a lute out of tune would yield to anyone, or in tune, to one who could not play. And yet in this wild ranging of the mind, a man may often perceive the way of it, and the dependence of one thought on another. For in a discussion of our present civil war, what could seem more impertinent than to ask (as someone did) what was the value of a Roman penny? Yet the coherence to me was clear enough. For the thought of the war introduced the thought of the delivering up of the King to his enemies; the thought of that brought in the thought of the delivering up of Christ; and that, again, the thought of the thirty pence, which was the price of that treason; and from that easily followed that malicious question—all this in a moment of time, for thought is quick.

The second sort is more constant, being regulated by some desire and design. For the impression made by such things as we desire or fear is strong and lasting—or, if it ceases for a time, of quick return: so strong sometimes as to hinder and break our sleep. From desire arises the thought of some means we have seen produce the like of what we aim at; and from the thought of that, the thought of means to that mean; and so continually, until we come to some beginning within our own power. And because the end, by the greatness of the impression, often comes to mind, in case our thoughts begin to wander, they are quickly brought back into the way; which one of the seven wise men, observing, made him give men this precept (now worn out): Respice Finem—that is, in all your actions, look often upon what you would have, as the thing that directs all your thoughts in the way to attain it.

The train of regulated thoughts is of two kinds. One is when, from an effect imagined, we seek the causes or means that produce it; and this is common to man and beast. The other is when, imagining anything whatsoever, we seek all the possible effects that can be produced by it; that is, we imagine what we can do with it once we have it. Of this I have at no time seen any sign except in man alone; for this is a curiosity hardly natural to any living creature that has no passion but the sensual, such as hunger, thirst, lust, and anger. In sum, the discourse of the mind, when it is governed by design, is nothing but seeking, or the faculty of invention, which the Latins call Sagacitas, and Solertia—a hunting out of the causes of some effect present or past, or of the effects of some present or past cause. Sometimes a man seeks what he has lost, and from the place and time at which he missed it, his mind runs back, from place to place and time to time, to find where and when he had it; that is, to find some certain and limited time and place at which to begin a method of seeking. Again, from there, his thoughts run over the same places and times, to find what action or other occasion might have made him lose it. This we call Remembrance, or Calling to Mind; the Latins call it Reminiscentia, as it were a re-conning of our former actions.

Sometimes a man knows a definite place within which he must seek; and then his thoughts run over all the parts of it, in the same way one would sweep a room to find a jewel, or as a spaniel ranges the field until he finds a scent, or as a man might run over the alphabet to find a rhyme.

Sometimes a man desires to know the outcome of an action; and then he thinks of some similar action in the past, and its outcomes one after another, supposing that like outcomes will follow like actions. As one who foresees what will become of a criminal reckons up what he has seen follow on the like crime before, having this order of thoughts: the Crime, the Officer, the Prison, the Judge, and the Gallows. This kind of thought is called Foresight, and Prudence, or Providence; and sometimes Wisdom—though such conjecture, through the difficulty of observing all circumstances, is very fallacious. But this is certain: by how much one man has more experience of things past than another, by so much also is he more prudent, and his expectations the more rarely fail him. The Present alone has a being in Nature; things past have a being only in the Memory; but things to come have no being at all, the Future being but a fiction of the mind, applying the consequences of actions past to actions present—which with most certainty is done by him who has most Experience, but not with certainty enough. And though it is called Prudence when the event matches our expectation, yet in its own nature it is but Presumption. For the foresight of things to come, which is Providence, belongs only to Him by whose will they are to come. From Him only, and supernaturally, proceeds Prophecy. The best prophet naturally is the best guesser; and the best guesser is he that is most versed and studied in the matters he guesses at, for he has the most signs to guess by.

A Sign is the antecedent event of the consequent, and conversely the consequent of the antecedent, when the like consequences have been observed before; and the oftener they have been observed, the less uncertain is the sign. And therefore he who has most experience in any kind of business has most signs by which to guess at future time, and is consequently the most prudent—and so much more prudent than he who is new in that kind of business, as not to be equalled by any advantage of natural and extempore wit, though many young men perhaps think the contrary.
Nevertheless, it is not Prudence that distinguishes man from beast. There are beasts that at a year old observe more, and pursue what is for their good, more prudently than a child can do at ten.

As Prudence is a presumption of the future, contracted from the experience of time past, so there is a presumption of things past taken from other things (not future but) also past. For he who has seen by what courses and degrees a flourishing state has first come into civil war, and then to ruin, upon the sight of the ruins of any other state will guess that the like war and the like courses have been there also. But his conjecture has almost the same uncertainty as the conjecture of the future, both being grounded only on experience.

There is no other act of man's mind, that I can remember, naturally planted in him, so as to need no other thing for its exercise but to be born a man and live with the use of his five senses. Those other faculties, of which I shall speak by and by, and which seem proper to man alone, are acquired and increased by study and industry, and of most men learned by instruction and discipline; and they all proceed from the invention of Words and Speech. For besides sense, and thoughts, and the train of thoughts, the mind of man has no other motion; though by the help of Speech and Method, the same faculties may be raised to such a height as to distinguish men from all other living creatures.

Whatever we imagine is finite. Therefore there is no idea, or conception, of anything we call Infinite. No man can have in his mind an image of infinite magnitude, nor conceive the ends and bounds of the thing named, having no conception of the thing but only of our own inability. And therefore the name of GOD is used, not to make us conceive him (for he is incomprehensible, and his greatness and power are inconceivable), but that we may honour him. Also, because whatever (as I said before) we conceive has been perceived first by sense, either all at once or by parts, a man can have no thought representing anything not subject to sense. No man, therefore, can conceive anything but he must conceive it in some place, and endowed with some determinate magnitude, and capable of being divided into parts; nor that anything is all in this place and all in another place at the same time; nor that two or more things can be in one and the same place at once: for none of these things ever have been, or can be, incident to sense, but are absurd speeches, taken on credit (without any meaning at all) from deceived philosophers, and deceived or deceiving Schoolmen.

title: Chapter 4. Of Speech
paragraphs: Printing, though an ingenious invention, is no great matter compared with the invention of letters. Who first discovered the use of letters is unknown. The man who first brought them into Greece, men say, was Cadmus, son of Agenor, king of Phoenicia. It was a useful invention for preserving the memory of times past and for binding together a mankind dispersed across so many distant regions of the earth — and a difficult one too, since it required close observation of the various motions of the tongue, palate, lips, and the other organs of speech, in order to mark each one with its own character. But the most noble and useful invention of all was speech itself, made up of names (or appellations) and their connection, by which men record their thoughts, recall them when they are past, and declare them to one another for mutual use and conversation. Without speech there would have been no commonwealth, no society, no contract, and no peace among men — no more than there is among lions, bears, and wolves. The first author of speech was God himself, who instructed Adam how to name the creatures he set before his eyes; for Scripture goes no further in this matter. But that much was enough to direct Adam to add more names as the experience and use of things gave him occasion, and to join them, step by step, in ways that made him understood. By this slow accumulation, over time, he gathered as much language as he found use for — though not as copious as an orator or philosopher needs. For I find nothing in Scripture from which we can directly or by consequence gather that Adam was taught the names of all figures, numbers, measures, colours, sounds, fancies, or relations — much less the grammatical names of words and speech, such as General, Special, Affirmative, Negative, Interrogative, Optative, Infinitive, all of which are useful; and least of all the words Entity, Intentionality, Quiddity, and the other significant terms of the Schools.

But all that language, gathered and expanded by Adam and his descendants, was lost again at the tower of Babel, when by God's hand every man was struck, for his rebellion, with forgetfulness of his former tongue. Driven thereby to scatter themselves into the various parts of the world, it could only be that the present diversity of tongues proceeded by degrees from that scattering — taught to each people, as need (the mother of all inventions) required, and growing more copious with time.

The general use of speech is to translate our mental discourse into verbal discourse — to turn the train of our thoughts into a train of words — and this serves two purposes. The first is to record the consequences of our thoughts, which would otherwise slip from memory and force us to do the work again; words allow them to be recalled by the marks they were tied to. In this first use, names serve as marks, or notes of remembrance. The second purpose comes when many people use the same words to signify, by their order and connection, what they conceive or think about each matter, and likewise what they desire, fear, or feel any other passion about; in this use, words are called signs. The special uses of speech are these. First, to record what we find, by reflection, to be the cause of anything present or past, and what we find present or past things may produce or bring about — which, in sum, is the acquiring of the arts. Second, to show others the knowledge we have attained — that is, to counsel and teach one another. Third, to make known to others our wills and intentions, so that we may have one another's mutual help. Fourth, to please and amuse ourselves and others by playing with our words, innocently, for pleasure or ornament.

To these uses there correspond four abuses. First, when men record their thoughts wrongly, through the inconstancy of the meaning of their words, and so register as their conception something they never actually conceived, deceiving themselves. Second, when they use words metaphorically — that is, in a sense other than the one those words were appointed for — and so deceive others. Third, when they declare with words that to be their will which is not. Fourth, when they use words to wound one another. For since nature has armed living creatures — some with teeth, some with horns, some with hands — to wound an enemy, it is only an abuse of speech to wound a man with the tongue; unless he is one whom we are obliged to govern, in which case it is not to wound but to correct and amend.
The way speech serves the remembrance of the consequence of causes and effects lies in the imposition of names, and in their connection.

Of names, some are proper — peculiar to one thing only — such as Peter, John, this man, this tree; and some are common to many things, such as man, horse, tree. Each of these, though only one name, is nevertheless the name of various particular things; and in respect of all of them taken together, it is called a universal. There is nothing universal in the world but names; the things named are every one of them individual and singular.

A universal name is imposed on many things because they resemble one another in some quality or other accident. And whereas a proper name brings to mind one thing only, a universal recalls any one of those many things.

Among universal names, some have wider and some narrower meaning, the wider taking in the narrower; some are of equal extent and take in each other reciprocally. For example, the name Body is wider than the word Man, and contains it; the names Man and Rational are of equal extent and contain one another. But here we must take notice that by a 'name' we do not always mean, as in grammar, one word only, but sometimes several words taken together as a circumlocution. All these words — He That In His Actions Observes The Laws Of His Country — make up a single name, equivalent to the one word Just.

By imposing names of wider or narrower significance, we turn the reckoning of the consequences of things imagined in the mind into a reckoning of the consequences of names. For example: a man who has no use of speech at all — one born and remaining perfectly deaf and dumb — if he sets a triangle before his eyes alongside two right angles (such as the corners of a square), may by reflection find that the three angles of that triangle equal the two right angles standing beside it. But if another triangle of a different shape is then shown to him, he cannot know without a fresh effort whether the three angles of that one are also equal to the same. By contrast, a man who has the use of words, once he notices that this equality followed not from the length of the sides, nor from any other particular feature of his triangle, but only from this — that the sides were straight and the angles three; and that this was all that made him call it a triangle — will boldly conclude, universally, that the same equality of angles holds in all triangles whatsoever, and will record his finding in these general terms: Every Triangle Has Its Three Angles Equal To Two Right Angles. In this way the consequence found in one particular case comes to be registered and remembered as a universal rule; our mental reckoning is discharged of time and place; we are spared all labour of the mind except the first; and what was found true Here and Now becomes true at All Times and in All Places.

The use of words for recording our thoughts is in nothing more evident than in counting. A natural fool, who could never learn the order of the numeral words — One, Two, Three — may note every stroke of the clock and nod at it, or say 'one, one, one,' but can never know what hour it strikes. There was, it seems, a time when those number-names were not yet in use, and men were forced to apply the fingers of one or both hands to the things they wanted to keep account of; this is plausibly why our numeral words, in any nation, run only to ten — in some only to five — and then begin again. And he who can count to ten, if he recites them out of order, will lose himself and not know when he is done. Much less will he be able to add, to subtract, or to carry out any of the other operations of arithmetic. So without words there is no possibility of reckoning numbers — much less of reckoning magnitudes, speeds, forces, and other things whose calculation is necessary to the being or the well-being of mankind.

When two names are joined together into a consequence, or affirmation — as in 'A man is a living creature,' or 'If he is a man, he is a living creature' — if the later name (living creature) signifies all that the former name (man) signifies, then the affirmation, or the consequence, is true; otherwise it is false. For true and false are attributes of speech, not of things. Where there is no speech, there is neither truth nor falsehood. There may be error — as when we expect what will not come, or suspect what has not been — but in neither of those cases can a man be charged with untruth.

Since truth then consists in the right ordering of names within our affirmations, a man who seeks precise truth must remember what each name he uses stands for, and place it accordingly — or else he will find himself entangled in his words, like a bird in lime-twigs: the more he struggles, the more he is stuck. This is why in geometry — the only science that it has so far pleased God to grant to mankind — men begin by settling the meanings of their words; this settling of meanings they call Definitions, and they place them at the very beginning of their reckoning.

From this it appears how necessary it is, for any man who aspires to true knowledge, to examine the definitions of earlier authors — either correcting them where they are carelessly set down, or making them himself. For errors in definitions multiply as the reckoning proceeds, and lead men into absurdities which at last they see but cannot avoid, unless they reckon again from the beginning, where the foundation of their errors lies. Hence it happens that those who trust to books do as men do who cast up many little sums into a great one, without considering whether those little sums were rightly cast up to begin with: when at last the error becomes visible, since they do not suspect their first grounds, they do not know how to clear themselves, but spend their time fluttering through their books — like birds that, entering by the chimney and finding themselves shut in a chamber, beat themselves against the false light of a glass window for want of wit to consider which way they came in. So the first use of speech lies in the right defining of names — which is the acquiring of science; and the first abuse lies in wrong definitions, or none at all — from which proceed all the false and senseless tenets that make those men who take their instruction from the authority of books, rather than from their own reflection, fall as far below the condition of ignorant men as men endowed with true science stand above it. For between true science and erroneous doctrine, ignorance is in the middle. Natural sense and imagination are not subject to absurdity; nature itself cannot err; and as men grow in abundance of language, they become either wiser than ordinary or madder than ordinary. Nor is it possible, without letters, for any man to become either excellently wise, or (unless his memory is damaged by disease, or by some defect of the organs) excellently foolish. For words are wise men's counters — they only reckon with them; but they are the money of fools, who value them by the authority of an Aristotle, a Cicero, a Thomas, or any other doctor whatever, so long as he is a man.

Whatever can enter into an account or be considered in a reckoning is subject to names — whatever can be added to another to make a sum, or subtracted from another to leave a remainder. The Latins called accounts of money rationes, and the activity of accounting ratiocinatio; what we, in bills or account books, call items they called nomina — that is, names; and from this, it seems, they extended the word ratio to the faculty of reckoning in everything else. The Greeks have only one word, logos, for both speech and reason — not because they thought there was no speech without reason, but because there is no reasoning without speech. The act of reasoning they called syllogism, which means summing up the consequences of one statement with another. And because the same things may enter into the account under different aspects, their names are (to show that variety) twisted and diversified. This diversity of names can be reduced to four general heads.

First, a thing may enter into the account as matter, or body — as Living, Sensible, Rational, Hot, Cold, Moved, Quiet — in all of which the word matter or body is understood. All such are names of matter.

Second, a thing may enter into the account, or be considered, in respect of some accident or quality we conceive to be in it: as Being Moved, Being So Long, Being Hot, and so on. Then, by a small change or twist on the name of the thing itself, we make a name for that accident which we are considering: for Living we put into the account Life; for Moved, Motion; for Hot, Heat; for Long, Length, and so on. All such names are names of the accidents and properties by which one matter, or body, is distinguished from another. These are called abstract names — because they are severed (not from matter, but) from the account of matter.

Third, we bring into the account the properties of our own bodies, by which we make this kind of distinction: when something is seen by us, we do not reckon the thing itself, but the sight, the colour, the idea of it in the imagination; when something is heard, we do not reckon the thing itself, but the hearing, or the sound, which is our conception of it through the ear. These are names of fancies.

Fourth, we bring into the account, consider, and give names to names themselves and to speeches. So General, Universal, Special, Equivocal are names of names. And Affirmation, Interrogation, Command, Narration, Syllogism, Sermon, Oration, and many other such terms, are names of speeches.

And this exhausts the variety of positive names — names imposed to mark something that exists in nature, or may be conceived by the mind of man: bodies that exist or may be conceived, the properties of bodies that exist or may be imagined, or words and speech.

There are also other names, called negative, which are marks that signify that a given word is not the name of the thing in question — such words as Nothing, No Man, Infinite, Inteachable, Three Want Four, and the like. These are still useful in reckoning, or in the correction of reckoning: they call to mind our past thoughts, even though they are not names of anything, because they make us refuse to admit names that are not rightly used.

All other names are merely insignificant sounds, and they come in two kinds. The first is when they are new, and yet their meaning has not been explained by definition. The Schoolmen and confused philosophers have coined plenty of these.

The second kind comes when men compound a name out of two names whose meanings are contradictory and inconsistent — such as the name an Incorporeal Body, or (the same thing) an Incorporeal Substance, and many more. For whenever an affirmation is false, the two names composing it, joined together into one, signify nothing at all. For example, if it is a false affirmation to say A Quadrangle Is Round, then the phrase Round Quadrangle signifies nothing — it is a mere sound. So too, if it is false to say that virtue can be poured, or blown up and down, then the phrases Infused Virtue or Inspired Virtue are as absurd and meaningless as Round Quadrangle. And you will hardly meet with a senseless and insignificant word that is not built out of some Latin or Greek term. A Frenchman seldom hears our Saviour called by the name Parole, but very often by the name Verbe — yet Verbe and Parole differ only in that one is Latin and the other French.

When a man, upon hearing a piece of speech, has those thoughts which the words of that speech, and their connection, were appointed and constituted to signify, then he is said to understand it — understanding being nothing but conception produced by speech. Therefore, if speech is peculiar to man (as, for all I know, it is), then understanding is peculiar to him as well. And so, for absurd and false affirmations, when they are universal, there can be no understanding — though many think they understand when they really only repeat the words quietly, or rehearse them in their mind.
What kinds of speech signify the appetites, aversions, and passions of the human mind, and the use and abuse of them, I shall treat when I have spoken of the passions themselves.

The names of those things that affect us — those that please and displease us — are of inconstant meaning in everyday conversation, because not all men are affected the same way by the same thing, nor is the same man at all times. For since all names are imposed to signify our conceptions, and all our affections are nothing but conceptions, then when we conceive the same things differently we can hardly avoid naming them differently. The nature of what we conceive may be the same; yet the variety in our reception of it — given different bodily constitutions and the prejudices of opinion — colours everything with the tincture of our own passions. And so in reasoning a man must beware of words which, besides signifying what we imagine of the nature of things, also signify the disposition and interest of the speaker — such as the names of virtues and vices. One man calls 'wisdom' what another calls 'fear'; one calls 'cruelty' what another calls 'justice'; one 'prodigality' what another 'magnanimity'; one 'gravity' what another 'stupidity'; and so on. Such names can never serve as true grounds of reasoning. Nor can metaphors and figures of speech — though these are less dangerous, because they openly profess their inconstancy, which the others do not.

title: Chapter 5. Of Reason, and Science
paragraphs: When a man reasons, he does nothing else but conceive a total sum from the addition of parcels, or conceive a remainder from the subtraction of one sum from another. When this is done with words, it amounts to conceiving the consequence of the names of all the parts as taking us to the name of the whole — or, from the names of the whole and one part, taking us to the name of the other part. And though in some matters (as with numbers) men name other operations besides adding and subtracting — multiplying and dividing — these are really the same: multiplication is only the addition of equal things together, and division is only the subtraction of one thing as often as we can. These operations apply not only to numbers but to all kinds of things that can be added together or taken one from another. As arithmeticians teach addition and subtraction in numbers, so geometers teach the same in lines, figures (solid and superficial), angles, proportions, times, degrees of speed, force, power, and the like; logicians teach the same in consequences of words — adding two names together to make an affirmation, two affirmations to make a syllogism, many syllogisms to make a demonstration, and from the sum (or conclusion) of a syllogism subtracting one proposition to find the other. Writers on politics add together compacts to find men's duties; lawyers add together laws and facts to find what is right and wrong in private actions. In short, wherever there is room for addition and subtraction, there is room for reason; and where these have no place, reason has nothing at all to do.

From all this we can define — that is, determine — what is meant by the word reason when we count it among the faculties of the mind. Reason, in this sense, is nothing but the reckoning (that is, the adding and subtracting) of the consequences of general names agreed on for marking and signifying our thoughts. I say marking when we reckon by ourselves, and signifying when we demonstrate or argue our reckonings to other men.

And just as in arithmetic unpractised men must, and even professional accountants may often, make mistakes and tally falsely, so in any other subject of reasoning the ablest, most attentive, and most practised men may deceive themselves and infer false conclusions. Not that reason itself is anything other than right reason — just as arithmetic is a certain and infallible art — but no one man's reason, nor the reason of any number of men, constitutes that certainty, any more than an account is well cast up just because a great many men have unanimously approved it. So when there is a controversy in an account, the parties must by their own consent set up, as right reason, the reason of some arbitrator or judge whose verdict they will both abide by — otherwise their controversy must either come to blows or remain undecided, for want of a right reason constituted by nature. The same holds in all debates whatsoever. When men who think themselves wiser than everyone else clamour and demand right reason for judge, yet ask only that matters be settled by no one's reason but their own, this is as intolerable in human society as it would be in a card game, after trumps have been turned, for a player to use as trump on every occasion whichever suit he most happens to hold. For that is just what they do who insist that each of their passions, as it gains sway in them, shall be taken for right reason — especially in their own quarrels. By the very claim they lay to right reason, they betray that they lack it.

The use and end of reason is not the finding of the sum, and the truth, of one or a few consequences remote from the first definitions and settled meanings of names, but to begin at those, and then proceed from one consequence to another. For there can be no certainty in the final conclusion without certainty in all the affirmations and negations on which it was grounded and inferred. When the head of a household, in going over the books, casts up the totals of all the bills of expense into one sum — without paying attention to how each bill is summed up by the persons who hand them in, or what he is paying for — he gains nothing more than if he had passed the whole account in bulk, trusting to the skill and honesty of every accountant under him. So too in reasoning about all other things: a man who picks up his conclusions on the authority of authors, and does not trace them back to the first items in every reckoning (which are the meanings of names settled by definitions) wastes his labour, and knows nothing — he only believes.

When a man reckons without the use of words — which can be done with particular things, as when, on seeing some object, we guess what was likely to have come before it or what is likely to follow from it — and what he thought likely to follow does not follow, or what he thought likely to have preceded did not precede, this is called ERROR, and even the most prudent men are subject to it. But when we reason in words of general meaning, and arrive at a general inference that is false, then though it is commonly called error, it is in fact an ABSURDITY, or senseless speech. For error is only a deception, a presumption that something is past or to come, where, even though it was not past or not to come, no impossibility could be discovered. But when we make a general assertion, then unless it is true, its very possibility cannot be conceived. And words by which we conceive nothing except the sound itself are the words we call absurd, insignificant, and nonsense. So if a man were to talk to me of a Round Quadrangle, or the Accidents Of Bread In Cheese, or Immaterial Substances, or of A Free Subject, A Free Will, or of anything as 'free' apart from being free from being hindered by opposition, I would not say that he was in error, but that his words were without meaning — that is to say, absurd.

I said earlier (in the second chapter) that man surpasses all other animals in this faculty: that when he conceives anything whatsoever, he is inclined to inquire into the consequences of it, and what effects he can produce with it. To that I now add a further degree of the same excellence: that he can use words to reduce the consequences he finds to general rules, called theorems or aphorisms; that is, he can reason, or reckon, not only in number but in all other things, where one thing can be added to or subtracted from another.

But this privilege is mitigated by another — the privilege of absurdity, to which no living creature is subject but man alone. And among men, those most subject to it are those who profess philosophy. For what Cicero somewhere says of them is true beyond doubt: there is nothing so absurd but that it may be found in the books of the philosophers. The reason is plain. Not one of them begins his reasoning from definitions, or from the explanation of the names he is about to use — a method that has been used only in geometry, whose conclusions have for that very reason been made indisputable.

The first cause of absurd conclusions I ascribe to lack of method: that they do not begin their reasoning from definitions, that is, from the settled meanings of their words — as if they could cast up an account without knowing the value of the numerals One, Two, and Three.

And since (as I noted in the previous chapter) all bodies enter into the account under various considerations, and since these considerations bear various names, various absurdities arise from the confused and ill-fitting way these names are connected in assertions. And so —

The second cause of absurd assertions I ascribe to assigning names of bodies to accidents, or of accidents to bodies — as when men say that Faith Is Infused, or Inspired, when nothing can be poured or breathed into anything but a body; or that Extension Is Body; or that Phantasms Are Spirits, and the like.

The third I ascribe to giving the names of the accidents of bodies outside us to the accidents of our own bodies — as when men say that The Colour Is In The Body, or The Sound Is In The Air, and the like.
The fourth, to giving the names of bodies to names or speeches — as when men say that There Are Things Universal, or that A Living Creature Is A Genus, or A General Thing, and so on.
The fifth, to giving the names of accidents to names and speeches — as when men say, The Nature Of A Thing Is In Its Definition, or A Man's Command Is His Will, and the like.

The sixth, to the use of metaphors, tropes, and other rhetorical figures in place of proper words. For though it is allowable to say in everyday speech (for example) The Road Goes, Or Leads, This Way Or That, or The Proverb Says This Or That — although roads cannot walk, and proverbs cannot speak — yet in reckoning and the search for truth such phrases are not to be admitted.

The seventh, to names that signify nothing but are picked up and learned by rote from the Schools — like Hypostatical, Transubstantiate, Consubstantiate, Eternal-now, and the rest of the cant of the Schoolmen.

For anyone who can avoid these things, it is not easy to fall into absurdity, unless it be through the length of an account, in which he may perhaps forget what went before. For by nature all men reason alike, and reason well, when their principles are good. For who is so stupid as both to err in geometry and to persist in it once another has shown him his mistake?

From this it appears that reason is not, like sense and memory, born in us, nor acquired only through experience (as prudence is); it is gained by industry — first in aptly imposing names, and second in arriving at a good and orderly method by which to proceed from the elements (which are names), to assertions made by the connection of one name to another, and then to syllogisms (which are the connections of one assertion to another), until we come to a knowledge of all the consequences of the names involved in the matter in hand. This is what men call SCIENCE. And whereas sense and memory are only knowledge of fact, which is past and irrevocable, science is knowledge of consequences, and of the dependence of one fact on another: by which, from what we can presently do, we know how to do something else when we choose, or the like another time. For when we see how a thing comes about — by what causes, and in what way — then whenever the like causes come within our power, we see how to make them produce the like effects.

Children, then, are not endowed with reason at all until they have attained the use of speech. They are called reasonable creatures only because of the apparent possibility that they will have the use of reason in time to come. And the greater part of grown men, though they have the use of reasoning a little way (for instance in counting to some degree), find it of little use in everyday life. In ordinary life they govern themselves, some better, some worse, according to differences of experience, quickness of memory, and inclinations to various ends — but above all according to good or bad fortune, and the errors of one another. As for science, or sure rules for their actions, they are so far from it that they do not know what it is. They have taken geometry for conjuring. And as for the other sciences, those who have not been taught their beginnings, and a little progress in them — enough to see how they are acquired and built up — are on this point like children who, having no notion of generation, are made to believe by the women that their brothers and sisters are not born but found in the garden.

And yet those who have no science are in a better and nobler condition, with their natural prudence, than men who, by faulty reasoning or by trusting those who reason wrongly, fall into false and absurd general rules. For ignorance of causes and of rules does not set men so far off their way as does reliance on false rules — taking for the causes of what they aspire to, things that are not the causes, but rather the causes of the opposite.

To conclude: the light of human minds is plain words, but only when they have first been snuffed clean and purged of ambiguity by exact definitions. Reason is the pace; the growth of science, the path; and the benefit of mankind, the end. By contrast, metaphors and senseless or ambiguous words are like ignes fatui — the will-o'-the-wisps — and to reason on them is to wander among innumerable absurdities, ending in quarrelling, sedition, or contempt.

As much experience is prudence, so much science is sapience. We commonly have a single word, wisdom, for both; yet the Latins always distinguished prudentia from sapientia, assigning the first to experience, the second to science. To bring out the difference more clearly: suppose one man is gifted with an excellent natural skill and dexterity in handling his weapons, and another, on top of that dexterity, has acquired a science of where he can strike or be struck by his opponent in every possible posture and guard. The ability of the first stands to the ability of the second as prudence stands to sapience — both useful, but the second infallible. But those who, trusting only in the authority of books, follow the blind blindly, are like the man who, trusting in the false rules of a master of fence, ventures rashly upon an adversary who either kills or shames him.

The signs of science are of two sorts: some certain and infallible, others uncertain. Certain, when he who claims the science of any matter can teach it — that is, plainly demonstrate its truth to another. Uncertain, when only some particular events bear out his claim, and on many occasions prove things to be as he says they must. The signs of prudence are all uncertain, because to observe by experience and remember every circumstance that might change the outcome is impossible. But in any matter where a man has no infallible science to proceed by, to give up his own natural judgement and be guided instead by general maxims read in authors — which are subject to many exceptions — is a sign of folly, and is generally scorned under the name of pedantry. Even those men who in councils of the commonwealth love to show off their reading in politics and history rarely behave that way in their domestic affairs, where their own interest is at stake; there they have prudence enough for their private matters. But in public they study the reputation of their own wit more than the success of another man's business.

title: Chapter 6. Of the Interior Beginnings of Voluntary Motions
paragraphs: COMMONLY CALLED THE PASSIONS, AND THE SPEECHES BY WHICH THEY ARE EXPRESSED.

There are in animals two kinds of motion peculiar to them. The first is called vital — begun in generation and continued without interruption through their whole life — such as the flow of the blood, the pulse, breathing, digestion, nutrition, excretion, and so on; these motions need no help from the imagination. The other is animal motion, otherwise called voluntary motion: walking, speaking, moving any of our limbs in the manner first imagined in our minds. That sense is a motion in the organs and inner parts of a man's body, caused by the action of the things we see, hear, and so on, and that fancy is only the residue of that same motion remaining after sense — this was already said in the first and second chapters. And because walking, speaking, and the like voluntary motions always depend on a preceding thought of where, which way, and what, it is plain that the imagination is the first inner beginning of all voluntary motion. Untrained people do not believe there is any motion at all where the thing moved is invisible, or where the space it is moved through is (for shortness) imperceptible; but that does not stop such motions from being real. For however small a space may be, what moves through a greater space (of which that small one is part) must first move through that small one. These small beginnings of motion within a man's body, before they appear as walking, speaking, striking, and the other visible actions, are commonly called ENDEAVOUR.

Endeavour, when it is toward something which causes it, is called APPETITE, or DESIRE — the latter being the general name, the former often restricted to mean the desire for food, namely hunger and thirst. When the endeavour is away from something, it is generally called AVERSION. The words appetite and aversion we have from the Latin; both signify motion — one of approaching, the other of retreating. So too do the Greek words for the same, horme and aphorme. Nature itself often forces upon men those truths at which, when they go searching for something beyond nature, they later stumble. For the Schools find no actual motion in mere appetite to walk or move; but because they must acknowledge some motion, they call it metaphorical motion. This is simply an absurd phrase: for though words may be called metaphorical, bodies and motions cannot.

What men desire, they are also said to LOVE; and they HATE the things they are averse to. So desire and love are the same thing, except that by 'desire' we always mean the absence of the object, and by 'love' most often its presence. Likewise, by 'aversion' we mean the absence of the object, and by 'hate' its presence.

Some appetites and aversions are born with us: the appetite for food, and the appetite for excretion and elimination (which can also, and more properly, be called aversions, from something we feel within our bodies), and a few others. The rest, the appetites for particular things, come from experience, and from the testing of those things' effects on ourselves or on others. For things we do not know at all, or do not believe to exist, we can have no further desire than to taste and try. But aversion we have not only for things we know have hurt us, but also for things we do not know whether they will hurt us or not.

Those things we neither desire nor hate, we are said to despise. CONTEMPT is nothing but an unwillingness, or a stubbornness of the heart, to be moved by the action of certain things — and it comes either from the heart's being already moved otherwise by more powerful objects, or from lack of experience of the things in question.

Because the constitution of a man's body is in continual change, it is impossible that the same things should always produce in him the same appetites and aversions — and much less can all men agree in desiring any one and the same object.

But whatever is the object of any man's appetite or desire — that is what, for his part, he calls Good; the object of his hatred and aversion he calls evil; and the object of his contempt he calls vile and beneath notice. For the words good, evil, and contemptible are always used relative to the person who uses them. Nothing is simply and absolutely so. There is no common rule of good and evil to be drawn from the nature of the objects themselves; the rule comes from the person of the man (where there is no commonwealth), or, where there is a commonwealth, from the person who represents it — or from an arbitrator or judge whom the disagreeing parties have by consent set up to have his verdict serve as the rule.

The Latin tongue has two words whose meanings approach those of good and evil, but are not precisely the same: pulchrum and turpe. The first signifies what by some visible sign promises good, the second what promises evil. In our own tongue we have no general words to express them, but for pulchrum we say in some cases fair, in others beautiful, or handsome, or gallant, or honourable, or comely, or amiable; and for turpe we say foul, deformed, ugly, base, nauseous, and the like, as the subject demands. All these words, in their proper places, signify nothing but the look, or the countenance, that promises good or evil. So there are three kinds of good: good in the promise, which is pulchrum; good in effect, as the end desired, which is called jucundum — delightful; and good as the means, which is called utile — profitable. And just as many kinds of evil: evil in the promise, which is what they call turpe; evil in effect and end, which is molestum — unpleasant, troublesome; and evil in the means, inutile — unprofitable, harmful.

In sense, what is really within us is (as I said before) only motion, caused by the action of external objects, although in appearance it is, to the sight, light and colour; to the ear, sound; to the nostril, odour, and so on. In the same way, when the action of one of these objects is continued from the eyes, ears, and other organs through to the heart, the real effect there is nothing but motion, or endeavour — which consists in appetite or aversion, toward or away from the moving object. But the appearance, or sense, of that motion is what we call either DELIGHT or TROUBLE OF MIND.

This motion which is called appetite — and which, in its appearance, is called delight and pleasure — seems to be a strengthening of vital motion, and a help to it. And so the things that caused delight were not improperly called jucunda, from juvando, helping or fortifying; and their opposites molesta, offensive, from their hindering and troubling the vital motion.

Pleasure, then (or delight) is the appearance, or the sense, of good; and trouble or displeasure is the appearance, or the sense, of evil. So every appetite, desire, and love is accompanied by some delight, more or less; and every hatred and aversion by some degree of displeasure and offence.

Some pleasures, or delights, arise from the sense of an object that is present — these may be called the pleasures of sense. (The word 'sensual,' used only by those who condemn them, has no place until there are laws.) Of this kind are all loadings and emptyings of the body, and everything pleasant in sight, hearing, smell, taste, or touch. Other pleasures arise from the expectation that comes from foreseeing the end, or the consequence, of things — whether those things, in the sense, please or displease. These are the pleasures of the mind of the man who draws those inferences, and are generally called JOY. In the same way, some displeasures occur in the sense, and are called PAIN; others in the expectation of consequences, and are called GRIEF.

These simple passions called appetite, desire, love, aversion, hate, joy, and grief have their names varied for various reasons. First, when they succeed one another, they are differently named according to men's opinion of how likely it is that they will get what they desire. Second, according to the object loved or hated. Third, according to several of them taken together. Fourth, according to the alteration or succession itself.
Hope — appetite, together with the opinion that we shall obtain, is called HOPE.
Despair — the same, without that opinion, is DESPAIR.
Fear — aversion, together with the opinion of hurt from the object, is FEAR.
Courage — the same, together with the hope of avoiding that hurt by resistance, is COURAGE.
Confidence — constant hope is CONFIDENCE in ourselves.
Diffidence — constant despair is DIFFIDENCE in ourselves.
Indignation — anger over a great hurt done to another, when we believe that hurt to have been done by injury, is INDIGNATION.
Benevolence — the desire of good for another is BENEVOLENCE, GOOD WILL, CHARITY. If extended to mankind in general, GOOD NATURE.

Covetousness — the desire of riches is COVETOUSNESS, a name always used in a tone of blame, because men contending for riches are displeased when others obtain them; though the desire in itself is to be blamed or allowed according to the means by which those riches are sought.
Ambition — the desire of office or precedence is AMBITION, also used in the worse sense, for the same reason just given.
Pusillanimity — the desire of things that contribute very little toward our ends, and the fear of things that are only minor hindrances, is PUSILLANIMITY.
Magnanimity — the disregard of little helps and hindrances is MAGNANIMITY.
Valour — magnanimity in the face of death or wounds is VALOUR, FORTITUDE.
Wretchedness — pusillanimity in the same circumstance is called WRETCHEDNESS, MISERABLENESS, or PARSIMONY, according to whether it is approved or disapproved.
Kindness — the love of persons for the sake of company is KINDNESS.
Natural Lust — the love of persons for pleasing the senses only is NATURAL LUST.
Luxury — the same love, acquired by rumination — that is, by the imagining of past pleasure — is LUXURY.

The Passion of Love; Jealousy — the love of one person singularly, together with the desire to be singularly loved in return, is THE PASSION OF LOVE. The same, together with the fear that the love is not mutual, is JEALOUSY.
Revengefulness — the desire to make another, by doing him hurt, condemn some act of his own, is REVENGEFULNESS.

Curiosity — the desire to know why, and how, is CURIOSITY. It belongs to no living creature but man, so that man is distinguished from the other animals not only by his reason but also by this singular passion. In other animals, the appetite for food and the other pleasures of sense are so dominant that they crowd out the care to know causes — which care is a lust of the mind, and one which, by the steady delight it takes in the continual and tireless generation of knowledge, surpasses the brief intensity of any bodily pleasure.

Religion, Superstition; True Religion — fear of an invisible power, either invented by the mind or imagined from publicly accepted tales, is RELIGION; if not publicly accepted, SUPERSTITION. And when the power imagined is truly as we imagine it, TRUE RELIGION.

Panic Terror — fear, without an apprehension of why or what, is PANIC TERROR, so named from the fables that make Pan its author. In truth there is always, in the man so frightened, some apprehension of the cause, while the rest of the crowd runs away by example — each supposing his neighbour to know why. This passion therefore arises only in a crowd or multitude of people.
Admiration — joy arising from the apprehension of novelty is ADMIRATION; it is proper to man, because it stirs up the appetite to know the cause.

Glory, Vainglory — joy arising from the imagining of one's own power and ability is that lift of the mind which is called GLORYING. If founded on the experience of his own past actions, it is the same as confidence; but if founded on the flattery of others, or merely supposed by himself for the delight of its consequences, it is called VAINGLORY — a name properly given, because well-founded confidence prompts attempt, whereas the mere supposing of power does not, and so is rightly called vain.
Dejection — grief arising from the opinion of one's lack of power is called dejection of mind.

The vainglory that consists in pretending to, or supposing in ourselves, abilities we know we do not have, is most common in young men, fed by the histories or fictions of gallant figures, and is often corrected by age and by employment.

Sudden Glory, Laughter — sudden glory is the passion that produces those grimaces called LAUGHTER. It is caused either by some sudden act of one's own that pleases one, or by the apprehension of some deformity in another, by comparison with which one suddenly applauds oneself. It happens most to those who are conscious of having the fewest abilities themselves, and who are forced to keep their own good opinion of themselves by noting the imperfections of others. So much laughter at the defects of others is a sign of pusillanimity. For one of the proper works of great minds is to help and free others from scorn, and to compare themselves only with the ablest.

Sudden Dejection, Weeping — on the contrary, sudden dejection is the passion that produces WEEPING; it is caused by the kinds of accidents that suddenly remove some powerful hope or some prop of one's power. Those most subject to it are those who rely principally on outside helps — women, and children. So some weep at the loss of friends, others at their unkindness, others at the sudden stop put to their thoughts of revenge by a reconciliation. But in every case, both laughter and weeping are sudden motions; custom takes them both away. For no man laughs at old jokes, or weeps for an old calamity.

Shame, Blushing — grief at the discovery of some lack of ability is SHAME, the passion that shows itself in BLUSHING; it consists in the apprehension of something dishonourable. In young men it is a sign of the love of a good reputation, and is praiseworthy; in old men it is a sign of the same, but because it comes too late, it is not praiseworthy.
Impudence — the contempt of a good reputation is called IMPUDENCE.

Pity — grief at the calamity of another is PITY, and it arises from the imagining that the same calamity might befall oneself. It is therefore also called COMPASSION, and in the phrase of our day, FELLOW-FEELING. And so for calamity arriving from great wickedness, the best men feel the least pity; and for any given calamity, those have least pity who think themselves least exposed to it.

Cruelty — contempt for, or little feeling about, the calamity of others is what men call CRUELTY, and it proceeds from a sense of security about one's own fortune. For that any man should take pleasure in the great harms of others, with no further end of his own, I do not conceive to be possible.

Emulation, Envy — grief at the success of a competitor in wealth, honour, or other good, if joined with an endeavour to push our own abilities to equal or surpass his, is called EMULATION; but joined with the endeavour to undermine or hinder a competitor, it is ENVY.

Deliberation — when in a man's mind appetites and aversions, hopes and fears, concerning one and the same thing arise by turns, and as the various good and evil consequences of doing or not doing the proposed thing come one after another into our thoughts — so that now we have an appetite for it, now an aversion to it; now hope of being able to do it, now despair or fear about attempting it — the whole running total of desires, aversions, hopes, and fears, continued until the thing is either done or thought impossible, is what we call DELIBERATION.

And so there is no deliberation about things past, since they manifestly cannot be changed; nor about things known to be impossible, or thought so, since men know or think such deliberation pointless. But about things impossible in fact, which we think possible, we may deliberate, not knowing the deliberation is in vain. It is called deliberation because it puts an end to the liberty we had of doing or not doing the thing, according to our own appetite or aversion.
This alternation of appetites, aversions, hopes, and fears is no less present in other living creatures than in man; and so beasts also deliberate.

Every deliberation is said to end when the thing being deliberated about is either done or thought impossible; for until then we keep our liberty of doing or not doing, according to our appetite or aversion.
